definition: Ampere 100, A GPU variant named after French mathematician and physicist André-Marie Ampère
details: Ampere 100, A GPU variant named after French mathematician and physicist André-Marie Ampère

explainer.lead: The Nvidia A100 is a data-center GPU accelerator built on the Ampere architecture and released on May 14, 2020. It combines general-purpose computing cores, specialized Tensor Cores, and high-bandwidth memory, with features that let one physical GPU be divided among multiple jobs.

tiers.eli5: The A100 is a powerful computer chip made by Nvidia for doing many calculations at once. Think of it as a huge workshop with thousands of workers and a special team for AI calculations; it can also be divided into as many as seven smaller workshops so different jobs can share it.
tiers.practitioner: Treat the A100 as the GA100-based Ampere accelerator with CUDA Compute Capability 8.0, not as equivalent to the GA10x-based GeForce 30 series. Its Tensor Cores support FP16, bfloat16, TF32, and FP64 with sparsity acceleration, while MIG can partition a GPU into up to seven instances. Check memory requirements against the 40 GB and 80 GB variants, and remember that SR-IOV support is specific to the A100.
tiers.paperLevel: The A100 is a GA100 Ampere GPU fabricated on TSMC's 7 nm FinFET process, with CUDA Compute Capability 8.0, 6912 FP32/INT32 CUDA cores, 3456 FP64 CUDA cores, and 19.5 teraflops of FP32 performance. The original configuration provides 40 GB of HBM2 memory at 1.6 TB/s, and an 80 GB version was also released. Its third-generation Tensor Cores support FP16, BF16, TF32, and FP64 with sparsity acceleration, and MIG supports spatial partitioning into no more than seven instances.

explainer.example: A DGX A100 server combines eight A100 accelerators with two 64-core AMD Rome 7742 CPUs and 1 TB of RAM. On a single A100, MIG can instead create up to seven GPU instances, allowing the accelerator's resources to be spatially partitioned.

usedIn.name: Nvidia DGX A100
usedIn.detail: The third-generation DGX server initially included eight A100 accelerators, two 64-core AMD Rome 7742 CPUs, 1 TB of RAM, and 15 TB of PCIe Gen 4 NVMe storage.

usedIn.name: Nvidia A100 80 GB
usedIn.detail: An 80 GB GA100-based version announced at SC20 on November 16, 2020, extending the original 40 GB accelerator line.

explainer.intuition: The A100 packs several kinds of parallel computation into one accelerator: CUDA cores handle general calculations, Tensor Cores accelerate supported matrix formats, and HBM2 supplies data at high bandwidth. MIG adds a different kind of flexibility by dividing the physical GPU into separate instances.
howItWorks: The GA100 chip is manufactured using TSMC's 7 nm FinFET process and implements CUDA Compute Capability 8.0.
Its 6912 FP32/INT32 and 3456 FP64 CUDA cores perform general parallel computation, reaching 19.5 teraflops of FP32 performance.
Third-generation Tensor Cores accelerate FP16, bfloat16, TF32, and FP64 operations, including sparsity acceleration.
HBM2 memory supplies the original 40 GB model with 1.6 TB/s of memory bandwidth, while NVLink 3.0 and PCI Express 4.0 provide connectivity.
Multi-instance GPU partitioning can divide an A100 into as many as seven instances.
explainer.whyItMatters: The A100 brings high FP32 and FP64 compute capacity, multiple Tensor Core precisions, and fast HBM2 memory together in one data-center accelerator. Its support for MIG and SR-IOV also makes sharing and virtualization part of the hardware design rather than treating the GPU only as one indivisible device.
misconceptions: The A100 is one Ampere-based data-center accelerator, not a name for the entire Ampere family, which also includes GeForce and workstation GPUs.
The original A100 has 40 GB of memory; the A100 80 GB is a separate variant announced on November 16, 2020.
Ampere is the microarchitecture name, while André-Marie Ampère is the French mathematician and physicist after whom it is named.
